Persistence of periodic traveling waves and Abelian integrals

Armengol Gasull, Anna Geyer and Víctor Mañosa Address: Departament de Matemàtiques, Edifici Cc, Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, 08193 Cerdanyola del Vallès, Barcelona, Spain.
  Centre de Recerca Matemàtica, Edifici Cc, Campus de Bellaterra, 08193 Cerdanyola del Vallès, Barcelona, Spain. Email address: gasull@mat.uab.cat Address: Delft Institute of Applied Mathematics, Faculty Electrical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Science Delft University of Technology, Van Mourik Broekmanweg 6, 2628 XE Delft, The Netherlands Email address: A.Geyer@tudelft.nl Address: Departament de Matemàtiques and Institut de Matemàtiques de la UPC-BarcelonaTech (IMTech), Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Colom 11, 08222 Terrassa, Spain Email address: victor.manosa@upc.edu
Abstract.

It is well known that the existence of traveling wave solutions (TWS) for many partial differential equations (PDE) is a consequence of the fact that an associated planar ordinary differential equation (ODE) has certain types of solutions defined for all time. In this paper we address the problem of persistence of TWS of a given PDE under small perturbations. Our main results deal with the situation where the associated ODE has a center and, as a consequence, the original PDE has a continuum of periodic traveling wave solutions. We prove that the TWS that persist are controlled by the zeroes of some Abelian integrals. We apply our results to several famous PDE, like the Ostrovsky, Klein-Gordon, sine-Gordon, Korteweg-de Vries, Rosenau-Hyman, Camassa-Holm, and Boussinesq equations.

Key words and phrases: 
Traveling wave, Abelian integral, Melnikov-Poincaré-Pontryagin function, periodic orbit, limit cycle, bifurcation
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 35C07; 34CO8. Secondary: 34C23, 34C25, 37C27.

1. Introduction

Traveling wave solutions (TWS) are an important class of particular solutions of partial differential equations (PDE). These waves are special solutions which do not change their shape and which propagate at constant speed. They appear in fluid dynamics, chemical kinetics involving reactions, mathematical biology, lattice vibrations in solid state physics, plasma physics and laser theory, optical fibers, etc. In these systems the phenomena of dispersion, dissipation, diffusion, reaction and convection are the fundamental physical common facts. We refer the reader to some interesting sources to know more details about the first appearance of this kind of solutions in the works of Russell (1834), Boussinesq (1877), Korteweg and de Vries (1895), Luther (1906), Fisher (1937), Kolmogorov, Petrovskii and Piskunov (1937), and to find several examples of applications and further motivation to study them: see [12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20, 23, 26, 28] and the references therein.

When studying ordinary differential equations (ODE), especially when they are modeling real world phenomena, it is very important to take into account whether the ODE are structurally stable. In a few words this means that if we fix a compact set 𝒦\mathcal{K} in the phase space it is said that an ODE is structurally stable on 𝒦\mathcal{K} when any other close enough (in the 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1}-topology) differential equation has a conjugated phase portrait. This concept is relevant for applications because it implies that the observed behaviours are qualitatively robust with respect to small changes of the model, see for instance [1, 24, 27] for more details, in particular concerning the planar case. Recall that the boundary of the sets of structurally stable differential equations is precisely where bifurcations (that is, qualitative changes of the phase portraits) may occur.

It is well-known that for many PDE the existence of TWS is established by proving the existence of a particular solution of a planar ordinary differential equation. These particular solutions must be defined for all time and, in the light of the previous definition, can roughly be classified into two categories:

  • •

    TWS created by a dynamical behaviour that is structurally stable. Examples of this situation are hyperbolic limit cycles or heteroclinic connections where both critical points are hyperbolic and one of them is a node.

  • •

    TWS created by a dynamical behaviour that is not structurally stable, as for instance continua of periodic orbits, or homoclinic or heteroclinic solutions connecting hyperbolic saddles.

In the first situation, simply take as the set 𝒦\mathcal{K} a compact neighbourhood of the orbit that gives rise to the TWS for a given PDE. Then it can be easily seen that a small enough 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} perturbation of the original PDE with the same order will still have a TWS. This is so because all the structurally stable phenomena in ODE are robust under 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1}-perturbations. The only condition that must be checked is that the 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1}-closeness between the two PDE’s is translated into a 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1}-closeness in 𝒦\mathcal{K} of the corresponding ODE.

An example corresponding to the first situation is the Fisher-Kolmogorov PDE, ut=ux​x+u⁡(1−u),u_{t}=u_{xx}+u(1-u), where the existence of several TWS of front type with different speeds is associated to the existence of a homoclinic connection between a hyperbolic saddle and a node, see [2, 13] and references therein. Therefore, all PDE of the form ut=ux​x+u⁡(1−u)+ε​g​(u,ux,ut,ε)u_{t}=u_{xx}+u(1-u)+\varepsilon g(u,u_{x},u_{t},\varepsilon) for ε\varepsilon small enough have such type of TWS. In fact, the same result holds for many perturbed Fisher-Kolmogorov PDE with a perturbation term of the form ε​g​(u,ux,ut,ux​x,ux​t,ut​t,ε)\varepsilon g(u,u_{x},u_{t},u_{xx},u_{xt},u_{tt},\varepsilon). As a second example of the first situation mentioned above, for some PDE of the form ut=ux​x+h⁡(u)​ux+g⁡(u)u_{t}=u_{xx}+h(u)u_{x}+g(u) there are periodic TWS which are associated to the existence of hyperbolic limit cycles, see for instance [8, 22] and the references therein.

In this paper we address the second, more delicate, situation. More specifically, we consider several PDE having a continuum of periodic TWS associated to a center of a second order ODE associated to the PDE, and we study which conditions have to be imposed on the perturbation of the PDE to be able to ensure that TWS persist and to quantify them.

We split our main results into two theorems, which we state in Section 2 after giving some preliminary definitions and notations. Our first result deals with second order PDE, see Theorem A, and applies to a wide range of equations. Our second result, Theorem B, is more restrictive on the one hand because it only considers some special perturbations, but on the other hand it applies to higher order PDE. In Section 3 we study a particular class of Abelian integrals that will often appear in the analysis of the perturbations in Section 4. For these Abelian integrals our main result is given in Theorem C. Finally, in Section 4 we detail some applications of our results. First, in Section 4.1, we apply Theorem A to perturbations of TWS of second order equations such as the Ostrovsky, Klein-Gordon and sine-Gordon equations. Afterwards, in Section 4.2 we use Theorem B to study perturbations of higher order PDE given by the Korteweg-de Vries, Rosenau-Hyman, Camassa-Holm, and Boussinesq equations.

Second order equations. Our main result applies to a certain class of perturbed PDE that satisfy three conditions (i)–(iii) that we detail below. Succinctly, it requires the existence of a certain wave speed c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} such that: (i) the associated ODE has the form U′′=fc​(U,U′)+ε​gc​(U,U′,ε)U^{\prime\prime}=f_{c}(U,U^{\prime})+\varepsilon g_{c}(U,U^{\prime},\varepsilon); (ii) after a time reparameterization if necessary the planar system associated with this ODE can be written as a perturbation of a Hamiltonian system; and (iii) this Hamiltonian system has a center, and the Melnikov-Poincaré-Pontryagin function associated with the perturbation has ℓ\ell simple zeroes, see [4, Part II] for further details.

Theorem A.

Assume that the second order PDE

(3) P⁡(u,ut,ux,ut​t,ut​x,ux​x,ε)=0,P(u,u_{t},u_{x},u_{tt},u_{tx},u_{xx},\varepsilon)=0,

satisfies Property 𝒜\mathcal{A} for some c∈ℝ.c\in\mathbb{R}. Then:

  1. (a)

    For ε=0\varepsilon=0 the PDE (3) has a continuum of periodic TWS, u=Uh​(x−c​t),u=U_{h}(x-ct), for hh in an open real interval.

  2. (b)

    For ε\varepsilon small enough it has at least ℓ\ell periodic TWS, u=Uhj(x−ct,ε),j=1,2,…,ℓ.u=U_{h_{j}}(x-ct,\varepsilon),j=1,2,\ldots,\ell.

{x′=d​xd​s=y,y′=d​xd​s=fc​(x,y)+ε​gc​(x,y,ε).\left\{\!\begin{array}[]{l}x^{\prime}=\dfrac{dx}{ds}=y,\\[10.0pt] y^{\prime}=\dfrac{dx}{ds}=f_{c}(x,y)+\varepsilon g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon).\end{array}\right.

When ε≠0\varepsilon\neq 0 is small enough we are in the setting of the perturbations of Hamiltonian systems, [4, 9]. Recall that for general perturbed 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} Hamiltonian systems,

(6) {x˙=∂H⁡(x,y)∂y+ε​R​(x,y,ε),y˙=−∂H⁡(x,y)∂x+ε​S​(x,y,ε),\begin{cases}\dot{x}=\phantom{-}\dfrac{\partial H(x,y)}{\partial y}+\varepsilon R(x,y,\varepsilon),\\[10.0pt] \dot{y}=-\dfrac{\partial H(x,y)}{\partial x}+\varepsilon S(x,y,\varepsilon),\end{cases}

Higher order equations (m>2m>2). In this situation our approach only works for a particular class of differential equations. Again, fixed (c,k)∈ℝ2,(c,k)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, we will define a property similar to Property 𝒜\mathcal{A} which will consist of four conditions. The first one, that we will call condition (o), is the most restrictive one and it is totally different to the ones imposed when m=2.m=2. It states that the associated ODE can somehow be reduced to a second order equation, or that some of the solutions of the associated ODE are also solutions of a related second order ODE. The rest of the conditions are quite similar to the ones of the planar case.

Theorem B.

Assume that the mm-th order PDE (1), with m>2,m>2, satisfies Property ℬ,\mathcal{B}, for some c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} and k∈ℝ.k\in\mathbb{R}. Then:

  1. (a)

    For ε=0\varepsilon=0 the PDE (3) has a continuum of periodic TWS, u=Uh,k​(x−c​t)u=U_{h,k}(x-ct) for hh in an open real interval.

  2. (b)

    For ε\varepsilon small enough it has at least ℓ\ell periodic TWS, u=Uhj,k​(x−c​t,ε)u=U_{h_{j},k}(x-ct,\varepsilon) for j=1,2,…,ℓ.j=1,2,\ldots,\ell.

Proof of Theorem B.

From condition (o) of Property ℬ,\mathcal{B}, if we restrict our attention to the solutions of (2) contained in

(7) Qc​(U,U′,U′′,ε)=k,Q_{c}(U,U^{\prime},U^{\prime\prime},\varepsilon)=k,

for the given value of k∈ℝ,k\in\mathbb{R}, we can find some TWS with speed cc and associated to this particular value of k.k. Other values of kk give different TWS with the same speed.

Starting from equation (7), instead of equation (4), we can repeat all the steps of the proof of Theorem A, point by point, to get the desired conclusion. ∎

3. Some particular Abelian integrals

This section is devoted to studying a particular class of Abelian integrals for which we prove a result quantifying their zeros, see Theorem C. We will use this result in the next section when we study the persistence of TWS for several perturbed PDE, which is governed by the number of zeros of integrals of this type.

Before proving the main result of this section, Theorem C, and to motivate one of its hypotheses, we collect some simple observations in the following lemma.

Lemma 3.2.

Let γ(h)⊂{H(x,y)=h}\gamma(h)\subset\{H(x,y)=h\}, h∈(0,h¯)=ℒ,h\in(0,\overline{h})=\mathcal{L}, be a continuum of periodic orbits surrounding a center, corresponding to h=0,h=0, of the Hamiltonian system associated to a 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} Hamiltonian function H⁡(x,y)H(x,y) and assume that they have a clockwise time parameterization. For each p,q∈ℕ∪{0},p,q\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, consider the Abelian integral

Jq,p​(h)=∫γ⁡(h)xq​yp​𝑑x.J_{q,p}(h)=\int_{\gamma(h)}x^{q}y^{p}\,dx.

The following holds.

  1. (a)

    When qq is even and pp is odd then Jq,p​(h)>0J_{q,p}(h)>0 for all h∈ℒ.h\in\mathcal{L}.

  2. (b)

    When qq is even and pp is even and H⁡(x,y)=H⁡(x,−y)H(x,y)=H(x,-y) then Jq,p​(h)≡0J_{q,p}(h)\equiv 0 on the whole interval ℒ.\mathcal{L}.

  3. (c)

    When qq is odd and pp is odd and H⁡(−x,y)=H⁡(x,y)H(-x,y)=H(x,y) then Jq,p​(h)≡0J_{q,p}(h)\equiv 0 on ℒ.\mathcal{L}.

Proof.

Notice that by Green’s theorem

Jq,p​(h)=∫γ⁡(h)xq​yp​𝑑x=∬Int⁡(γ⁡(h))p​xq​yp−1​𝑑x​𝑑y,J_{q,p}(h)=\int_{\gamma(h)}x^{q}y^{p}\,dx=\iint_{\operatorname{Int}(\gamma(h))}px^{q}y^{p-1}\,dx\,dy,

where Int⁡(γ⁡(h))\rm{Int}(\gamma(h)) denotes the interior of the oval. Then, trivially (a)(a) follows. The other two statements are consequence of the symmetries of HH and the function xq​yp−1.x^{q}y^{p-1}. ∎

The next proposition will be one of the key results to prove Theorem C, which is stated below.

Proposition 3.3.

([6]) Set ℒ⊂ℝ\mathcal{L}\subset\mathbb{R} an open real interval and let Fj:ℒ→ℝ,F_{j}:\mathcal{L}\to\mathbb{R}, j=0,1,…,ℓ,j=0,1,\ldots,\ell, be ℓ+1\ell+1 linearly independent analytic functions. Assume also that one of them, say Fk,0≤k≤ℓ,F_{k},0\leq k\leq\ell, has constant sign on ℒ.\mathcal{L}. Then, there exist real constants dj,d_{j}, j=0,1,…,ℓ,j=0,1,\ldots,\ell, such that the linear combination ∑j=0ℓdj​Fj\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}d_{j}F_{j} has at least ℓ\ell simple zeroes in ℒ.{\mathcal{L}}.

Notice that in the next theorem, and due to Lemma 3.2, the monomials of the Abelian integral that we consider are of the form x2​q​y2​p−1.x^{2q}y^{2p-1}.

Theorem C.

Let H⁡(x,y)=A⁡(x)​y2+B⁡(x),H(x,y)=A(x)y^{2}+B(x), with AA and BB functions satisfying the hypotheses of Proposition 3.1, and denote by γ⁡(h),\gamma(h), h∈(0,h¯),h\in(0,\overline{h}), the periodic orbits surrounding the origin of the corresponding Hamiltonian system. For d0,d1,…,dn∈ℝd_{0},d_{1},\ldots,d_{n}\in\mathbb{R} and qj,pj∈ℕ,j=0,1,…,ℓq_{j},p_{j}\in\mathbb{N},j=0,1,\ldots,\ell consider the family of Abelian integrals

J⁡(h)=∫γ⁡(h)∑j=0ℓdj​x2​qj​y2​pj−1​𝑑x.J(h)=\int_{\gamma(h)}\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}d_{j}x^{2q_{j}}y^{2p_{j}-1}\,dx.

If all values mj=qj+pj,j=0,1,…,ℓm_{j}=q_{j}+p_{j},j=0,1,\ldots,\ell are different, there exit values of dj,j=0,1,…,ℓ,d_{j},j=0,1,\ldots,\ell, such that the corresponding function J⁡(h)J(h) has at least ℓ\ell simple zeroes in (0,h¯).(0,\overline{h}).

Proof.

Notice that

J⁡(h)=∑j=0ℓdj​Jj​(h),whereJj​(h)=∫γ⁡(h)x2​qj​y2​pj−1​𝑑x.J(h)=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}d_{j}J_{j}(h),\quad\mbox{where}\quad J_{j}(h)=\int_{\gamma(h)}x^{2q_{j}}y^{2p_{j}-1}\,dx.

By Proposition 3.1, for each j=0,1,…,ℓ,j=0,1,\ldots,\ell, Jj​(h)=kj​hmj+o⁡(hmj)J_{j}(h)=k_{j}h^{m_{j}}+o\big(h^{m_{j}}\big) and, by hypothesis, all these mjm_{j} are different. This clearly implies that all these ℓ+1\ell+1 functions are linearly independent. Moreover, by item (a)(a) of Lemma 3.2 we know that none of them vanish in (0,h¯).(0,\overline{h}). Hence we can apply Proposition 3.3 to this set of functions and ℒ=(0,h¯)\mathcal{L}=(0,\overline{h}) and the result follows. ∎

4. Applications

In this section we consider perturbations of several relevant PDE with continua of periodic TWS and prove that the perturbations can be tailored such that a prescribed number of TWS persist in these perturbed PDE. In many examples, for simplicity, we perturb the PDE with an additive term that only contains partial derivatives up to m−1.m-1. For more general perturbations, even including terms of order m,m, most of the results can be adapted.

4.1. Second order PDE

We start with an illustrative toy example for which we give all the details on how a prescribed number of periodic TWS can be obtained.

4.1.1. A toy example

Consider the PDE

(11) u+a​ux​x+b​ux​t+d​ut​t+ε​g​(ux,ut,ε)=0,u+au_{xx}+bu_{xt}+du_{tt}+\varepsilon g(u_{x},u_{t},\varepsilon)=0,

with gg a 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} function and take cc such that a−b​c+d​c2>0.a-bc+dc^{2}>0. Then equation (2) can be written as

U+(a−b​c+d​c2)​U′′+ε​g​(U′,−c​U′,ε)=0.U+(a-bc+dc^{2})U^{\prime\prime}+\varepsilon g(U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)=0.

We define C2=a−b​c+d​c2C^{2}=a-bc+dc^{2} and gc(U′,ε)=−g(U′,−cU′,ε)/C2.g_{c}(U^{\prime},\varepsilon)=-g(U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)/C^{2}. Then it is easy to see that this PDE satisfies Property 𝒜\mathcal{A} with Hc​(x,y)=x2/(2​C2)+y2/2,H_{c}(x,y)=x^{2}/(2C^{2})+y^{2}/2, sc​(x,y)≡1s_{c}(x,y)\equiv 1 and (0,h¯)=(0,∞).(0,\overline{h})=(0,\infty). That is,

{x˙=∂Hc​(x,y)∂y=y,y˙=−∂Hc​(x,y)∂x+ε​gc​(x,y,ε)=−xC2+ε​gc​(y,ε).\begin{cases}\dot{x}=\phantom{-}\dfrac{\partial H_{c}(x,y)}{\partial y}=y,\\[10.0pt] \dot{y}=-\dfrac{\partial H_{c}(x,y)}{\partial x}+\varepsilon g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon)=-\dfrac{x}{C^{2}}+\varepsilon g_{c}(y,\varepsilon).\end{cases}

Moreover

Mc​(h)=∫γ⁡(h)gc​(y,0)​𝑑x,M_{c}(h)=\int_{\gamma(h)}g_{c}(y,0)\,dx,

where γ⁡(h)\gamma(h) is the ellipse {x2/(2C2)+y2/2=h}.\{x^{2}/(2C^{2})+y^{2}/2=h\}. We parameterize the closed curves Hc​(x,y)=hH_{c}(x,y)=h as (x,y)=(C​2​h​cos⁡θ,2​h​sin⁡θ)(x,y)=(C\sqrt{2h}\cos\theta,\sqrt{2h}\sin\theta) for 0≤θ≤2​π.0\leq\theta\leq 2\pi. Then

Mc(h)=−C2​h∫02​πgc(2​hsinθ,0)sinθdθ.M_{c}(h)=-C\sqrt{2h}\int_{0}^{2\pi}g_{c}(\sqrt{2h}\sin\theta,0)\sin\theta\,d\theta.

Assume for instance that gc​(y,0)=∑j=0Ngj​yjg_{c}(y,0)=\sum_{j=0}^{N}g_{j}y^{j} is a polynomial of degree NN, and gj∈ℝg_{j}\in\mathbb{R}. Then,

Mc(h)=−C2​h∑j=0Ngj(2​h)j(∫02​πsinj+1θdθ).M_{c}(h)=-C\sqrt{2h}\sum_{j=0}^{N}g_{j}(\sqrt{2h})^{j}\Big(\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sin^{j+1}\theta\,d\theta\Big).

When jj is even, by symmetry, the above integrals vanish. Hence

Mc​(h)=−2​C​h​(∑i=0[(N−1)/2]g2​i+1​2i​I2​i+2​hi),M_{c}(h)=-2Ch\Big(\sum_{i=0}^{[(N-1)/2]}g_{2i+1}2^{i}I_{2i+2}h^{i}\Big),

where [⋅][\,\cdot\,] denotes the integer part and I2​n=∫02​πsin2​n⁡θ​𝑑θ>0.I_{2n}=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sin^{2n}\theta\,d\theta>0. Removing the factor hh, and taking suitable g2​i+1g_{2i+1}, the polynomial Mc​(h)/hM_{c}(h)/h can be any arbitrary polynomial of degree [(N−1)/2][(N-1)/2] in hh. Hence, by applying Theorem C, for any ℓ≤[(N−1)/2],\ell\leq[(N-1)/2], there exist coefficients gjg_{j} such that the function Mc​(h)M_{c}(h) has ℓ\ell simple zeros and, therefore, by applying Theorem A, the PDE (11) has at least ℓ\ell periodic TWS. We remark that the above computations are essentially the same as the ones of the celebrated paper [21] where the authors present the first example of classical polynomial Liénard differential system of degree NN with [(N−1)/2][(N-1)/2] limit cycles.

By doing similar computations we can consider more general perturbations in PDE (11), like for instance

u+a​ux​x+b​ux​t+d​ut​t+ε⁡(u​ux​x+g⁡(u,ux,ut,ε))=0,u+au_{xx}+bu_{xt}+du_{tt}+\varepsilon(uu_{xx}+g(u,u_{x},u_{t},\varepsilon))=0,

and similar results hold.

4.1.2. Reduced Ostrovsky equation.

We consider perturbations of the reduced Ostrovsky equation, introduced by L. Ostrovsky in 1978, which is a modification of the Korteweg-de Vries equation that models gravity waves propagating in a rotating background under the influence of the Coriolis force when the high-frequency dispersion is neglected. More concretely, we take

(12) (ut+u​ux)x−u+ε​g​(u,ux,ut,ε)=0,(u_{t}+uu_{x})_{x}-u+\varepsilon g(u,u_{x},u_{t},\varepsilon)=0,

which satisfies Property 𝒜\mathcal{A} with c>0,c>0, because its associated ODE is

(U−c)​U′′+(U′)2−U+ε​g​(U,U′,−c​U′,ε)=0.(U-c)U^{\prime\prime}+(U^{\prime})^{2}-U+\varepsilon g(U,U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)=0.

Then, taking gc(U,U′,ε)=−g(U,U′,−cU′,ε)/(U−c);g_{c}(U,U^{\prime},\varepsilon)=-g(U,U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)/(U-c); 𝒱c={x<c};\mathcal{V}_{c}=\{x<c\}; xc=0;x_{c}=0; and sc​(x,y)=(x−c)−2s_{c}(x,y)=(x-c)^{-2}, the system that has to be studied to find TWS is

{x˙=∂Hc​(x,y)∂y,y˙=−∂Hc​(x,y)∂x+(x−c)2​ε​gc​(x,y,ε).\begin{cases}\dot{x}=\phantom{-}\dfrac{\partial H_{c}(x,y)}{\partial y},\\[10.0pt] \dot{y}=-\dfrac{\partial H_{c}(x,y)}{\partial x}+(x-c)^{2}\varepsilon g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon).\end{cases}

with

Hc​(x,y)=(x−c)2​y22+c​x22−x33.H_{c}(x,y)=\frac{(x-c)^{2}y^{2}}{2}+\frac{cx^{2}}{2}-\frac{x^{3}}{3}.

Consider also the Melnikov-Poincaré-Pontryagin function

Mc​(h)=∫γc​(h)(x−c)2​gc​(x,y,0)​𝑑x,h∈(0,c3/3).M_{c}(h)=\int_{\gamma_{c}(h)}(x-c)^{2}g_{c}(x,y,0)\,dx,\,h\in(0,c^{3}/3).

As in the toy example, it is not difficult to find a perturbation term gg such that the the function Mc​(h)M_{c}(h) has several simple zeroes in (0,c3/3)(0,c^{3}/3) which, by Theorem C, give rise to periodic TWS of the PDE (12).

4.1.3. Perturbed non-linear Klein-Gordon equation.

The Klein-Gordon equation is a wave equation related to the Schrödinger equation, which is used to model spinless relativistic particles. It was introduced in 1926 in parallel by O. Klein, W. Gordon and V. Fock as a tentative to describe the relativistic electron dynamics. In the one-dimensional setting we look at a perturbation of this equation of the form

ut​t−ux​x+λ​up+ε​g​(u,ux,ut,ε)=0,u_{tt}-u_{xx}+\lambda u^{p}+\varepsilon g(u,u_{x},u_{t},\varepsilon)=0,

with λ∈ℝ+\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{+} and pp an odd integer. It can readily be seen that it satisfies Property 𝒜\mathcal{A} and that the system that has to be studied to find TWS is

{x˙=∂Hc​(x,y)∂y,y˙=−∂Hc​(x,y)∂x+ε​gc​(x,y,ε),\begin{cases}\dot{x}=\phantom{-}\dfrac{\partial H_{c}(x,y)}{\partial y},\\[10.0pt] \dot{y}=-\dfrac{\partial H_{c}(x,y)}{\partial x}+\varepsilon g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon),\end{cases}

where

Hc​(x,y)=C​xp+1p+1+y22,H_{c}(x,y)=\frac{Cx^{p+1}}{p+1}+\frac{y^{2}}{2},

with C=λ/(c2−1),C=\lambda/(c^{2}-1), gc(x,y,ε)=−g(x,y,−cy,ε)/(c2−1).g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon)=-g(x,y,-cy,\varepsilon)/(c^{2}-1). The associated Melnikov-Poincaré-Pontryagin function is

Mc​(h)=∫γc​(h)gc​(x,y,0)​𝑑x,h∈(0,∞).M_{c}(h)=\int_{\gamma_{c}(h)}g_{c}(x,y,0)\,dx,\quad h\in(0,\infty).

The interested reader can take a look to the papers [5, 17] where perturbations of this Hamiltonian system and the zeros of its associated Melnikov-Poincaré-Pontryagin function are studied with two different approaches.

In particular, the zeroes of the above first integral can be studied in a similar way to the toy example considered at the beginning of this section. Notice, however, that when p≥3p\geq 3, instead of using trigonometric functions to parametrize the invariant closed curves, one can use the generalized polar coordinates introduced by Lyapunov in 1893 in his study of the stability of degenerate critical points, [19]. All the details can be found in [5]. Again, Theorem A guarantees that the zeros of the function Mc​(h)M_{c}(h) correspond with periodic TWS of the Klein-Gordon equation.

4.1.4. Perturbed sine-Gordon equation.

The sine-Gordon equation first appeared in 1862 in the context of differential geometry. Specifically in a study by E. Bour on surfaces of constant negative curvature. The equation was rediscovered later by J. Frenkel and T. Kontorova in 1939, in their study of crystal dislocations. The equation is relevant to the community investigating integrable systems because it has soliton solutions. Its perturbation writes as

ut​t−ux​x+sin⁡u+ε​g​(u,ux,ut,ε)=0.u_{tt}-u_{xx}+\sin u+\varepsilon g(u,u_{x},u_{t},\varepsilon)=0.

Again, it satisfies Property 𝒜\mathcal{A} for c>1,c>1, and its associated planar system is

{x˙=∂Hc​(x,y)∂y,y˙=−∂Hc​(x,y)∂x+ε​gc​(x,y,ε),\begin{cases}\dot{x}=\phantom{-}\dfrac{\partial H_{c}(x,y)}{\partial y},\\[10.0pt] \dot{y}=-\dfrac{\partial H_{c}(x,y)}{\partial x}+\varepsilon g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon),\end{cases}

where

Hc​(x,y)=C⁡(1−cos⁡x)+y22,H_{c}(x,y)={C(1-\cos x)}+\frac{y^{2}}{2},

with C=1/(c2−1)>0C=1/(c^{2}-1)>0 and gc​(x,y,ε)=g⁡(x,y,−c​y,ε)/(1−c2).g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon)=g(x,y,-cy,\varepsilon)/(1-c^{2}). The Melnikov-Poincaré-Pontryagin function is

Mc​(h)=∫γc​(h)gc​(x,y,0)​𝑑x,h∈(0,2​C).M_{c}(h)=\int_{\gamma_{c}(h)}g_{c}(x,y,0)\,dx,\quad h\in(0,2C).

The above type integrals are studied for instance in [11]. There, several condition on gg for obtaining many simple zeroes of McM_{c}, and therefore periodic TWS of the considered PDE, are obtained.

4.2. PDE with order greater than 2

In this section we study perturbations of several PDE with order m>2.m>2. We start with the following result that helps us to characterize the existence of centers for the unperturbed Hamiltonian systems that will appear.

Lemma 4.1.

Consider a Hamiltonian system of the form

{x˙=∂H⁡(x,y)∂y=y​m​(x,y),y˙=−∂H⁡(x,y)∂x=f⁡(x,y)​m​(x,y),\begin{cases}\dot{x}=\dfrac{\partial H(x,y)}{\partial y}=y\,m(x,y),\\[10.0pt] \dot{y}=-\dfrac{\partial H(x,y)}{\partial x}=f(x,y)\,m(x,y),\end{cases}

where H∈𝒞2H\in\mathcal{C}^{2}, m⁡(x,y)>0m(x,y)>0 and such that ∂∂x​(y​m​(x,y))+∂∂y​(f⁡(x,y)​m​(x,y))≡0.\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(ym(x,y)\right)+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(f(x,y)m(x,y)\right)\equiv 0. Then, a singular point of the form (x∗,0)(x_{*},0) is a center if

(13) ∂∂x​f​(x,y)|(x∗,0)<0.\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,y)\Big|_{(x_{*},0)}<0.

Furthermore, if m⁡(x,y)m(x,y) depends only on xx, condition (13) holds, and HH is analytic, then the Hamiltonian HH satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition 3.1.

Proof.

Consider the vector field X=(Hy,−Hx)X=(H_{y},-H_{x}). Since

det(D​X​(x∗,0))=−m2​(x∗,0)​∂∂x​(f⁡(x,y))|(x∗,0),\det(\mathrm{D}X(x_{*},0))=-m^{2}(x_{*},0)\,\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(f(x,y)\right)\Big|_{(x_{*},0)},

then equation (13) implies that det(D​X​(x∗,0))>0\det(\mathrm{D}X(x_{*},0))>0 and therefore (x∗,0)(x_{*},0) is a center (once more, remember that a singular point of a Hamiltonian system cannot be neither a focus nor a node).

If m⁡(x,y)=m⁡(x)m(x,y)=m(x), then H⁡(x,y)=y2​m​(x)/2+B⁡(x)H(x,y)=y^{2}\,m(x)/2+B(x) for some analytic function B.B. Since m⁡(x)>0m(x)>0 we can write m⁡(x)=2​a2+O⁡(x−x∗)m(x)=2a^{2}+O(x-x_{*}) near x=x∗.x=x_{*}. Suppose that condition (13) holds, then Hx​x​(x∗,0)=−fx​(x∗,0)​m​(x∗)>0H_{xx}(x_{*},0)=-f_{x}(x_{*},0)m(x_{*})>0, and we can write 1/b2=B′′​(x∗)=Hx​x​(x∗,0)1/b^{2}=B^{\prime\prime}(x_{*})=H_{xx}(x_{*},0), obtaining B⁡(x)=(x−x∗)2/b2+O⁡((x−x∗)3)B(x)=(x-x_{*})^{2}/b^{2}+O\big((x-x_{*})^{3}\big). So HH fulfills the hypotheses of Proposition 3.1. ∎

Observe that condition (13) is equivalent to the fact that Hx​x​(x∗,0)>0H_{xx}(x_{*},0)>0 and det(𝐇H​(x∗,0))>0\det(\mathbf{H}_{H}(x_{*},0))>0 (where 𝐇\mathbf{H} is the hessian matrix), which implies that HH has a non-degenerate local minimum at (x∗,0)(x_{*},0).

4.2.1. Perturbed generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation

We consider a perturbation of a family of PDE which for certain values of the parameters contains the celebrated Korteweg-de Vries and Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equations appearing in several domains of physics (non-linear mechanics, water waves, etc.). More concretely, we consider the family of PDE

(14) ut+a​ux+b​u​ux+d​u​ut+p​ux​x​x+q​ux​x​t+r​ux​t​t+s​ut​t​t+ε∇g(u,ux,ut,ε)⋅(ux,ux​x,ux​t,0)t=0.u_{t}+au_{x}+buu_{x}+duu_{t}+pu_{xxx}+qu_{xxt}+ru_{xtt}+su_{ttt}\\ +\varepsilon\nabla g(u,u_{x},u_{t},\varepsilon)\cdot(u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xt},0)^{t}=0.

Notice that the KdV equation corresponds to ε=0\varepsilon=0 and a=d=q=r=s=0,a=d=q=r=s=0, b=−6b=-6 and p=1.p=1. The ODE associated to (14) is

((a−c)​U+b−d​c2​U2+C​U′′+ε​g​(U,U′,−c​U′,ε))′=0,\Big((a-c)U+\frac{b-dc}{2}{U^{2}}+CU^{\prime\prime}+\varepsilon g(U,U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)\Big)^{\prime}=0,

where C=p−q​c+r​c2−s​c3.C=p-qc+rc^{2}-sc^{3}. Notice that then, for any function UU satisfying previous equation, it holds that there exists k∈ℝ,k\in\mathbb{R}, such that

(15) (a−c)​U+b−d​c2​U2+C​U′′+ε​g​(U,U′,−c​U′,ε)=k(a-c)U+\frac{b-dc}{2}{U^{2}}+CU^{\prime\prime}+\varepsilon g(U,U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)=k

Thus we have to study the equivalent planar system

{x˙=y=∂Hc,k​(x,y)∂y,y˙=αc,k+βc​x+γc​x2+ε​gc​(x,y,ε)=−∂Hc,k​(x,y)∂x+ε​gc​(x,y,ε),\begin{cases}\dot{x}=y=\dfrac{\partial H_{c,k}(x,y)}{\partial y},\\[10.0pt] \dot{y}=\alpha_{c,k}+\beta_{c}x+\gamma_{c}x^{2}+\varepsilon g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon)=-\dfrac{\partial H_{c,k}(x,y)}{\partial x}+\varepsilon g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon),\end{cases}

where

Hc,k​(x,y)=−αc,k​x−βc2​x2−γc3​x3+12​y2,H_{c,k}(x,y)=-\alpha_{c,k}x-\frac{\beta_{c}}{2}x^{2}-\frac{\gamma_{c}}{3}x^{3}+\frac{1}{2}y^{2},

with

αc,k=kC,βc=c−aC,γc=d​c−bC,\alpha_{c,k}=\frac{k}{C},\quad\beta_{c}=\frac{c-a}{C},\quad\gamma_{c}=\frac{dc-b}{C},

and gc(x,y,ε)=−g(x,y,−cy,ε)/C.g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon)=-g(x,y,-cy,\varepsilon)/C. Hence, using Lemma 4.1, it is not difficult to see that the PDE (14) satisfies Property ℬ\mathcal{B} when equation αc,k+βc​x+γc​x2=0\alpha_{c,k}+\beta_{c}x+\gamma_{c}x^{2}=0 has two different real solutions (that correspond to a center and a saddle of the planar system). Then, by Theorem B, the periodic TWS that persist for ε\varepsilon small enough correspond to the simple zeroes of the elliptic integral

Mc,k​(h)=∫γc,k​(h)gc​(x,y,0)​𝑑xM_{c,k}(h)=\int_{\gamma_{c,k}(h)}g_{c}(x,y,0)\,dx

in a suitable open interval of energies. This kind of Abelian integrals are studied in detail in the classical paper of Petrov ([25]) and more recently in the Chapter 3 of Part II of the book [4]. Again, it is not difficult to impose conditions on gg to get a prescribed number of TWS for (14) for ε\varepsilon small enough and different values of cc and k.k.

4.2.2. Perturbed Rosenau-Hyman equation

The Rosenau-Hyman equation is a generalization of the KdV equation. It was introduced in 1993 by P. Rosenau and J.M. Hyman to show the existence of solitary waves with compact support (compactons) in the context of non-linear dispersive equations. We consider the perturbed equation

ut+a(un)x+(un)x​x​x+ε∇g(u,ux,ut,ε)⋅(ux,ux​x,ux​t,0)t=0,u_{t}+a(u^{n})_{x}+(u^{n})_{xxx}+\varepsilon\nabla g(u,u_{x},u_{t},\varepsilon)\cdot(u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xt},0)^{t}=0,

where a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R} and n∈ℕ.n\in\mathbb{N}. To find TWS for it we have to study the third order ODE

−\displaystyle- cU′+a(Un)′+(Un)′′′+ε∇g(U,U′,−cU′,ε)⋅(U′,U′′,−cU′′,0)t\displaystyle cU^{\prime}+a(U^{n})^{\prime}+(U^{n})^{\prime\prime\prime}+\varepsilon\nabla g(U,U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)\cdot(U^{\prime},U^{\prime\prime},-cU^{\prime\prime},0)^{t}
=(−c​U+a​Un+(Un)′′+ε​g​(U,U′,−c​U′,ε))′\displaystyle=\big(-cU+aU^{n}+(U^{n})^{\prime\prime}+\varepsilon g(U,U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)\big)^{\prime}
=(−c​U+a​Un+n⁡(n−1)​Un−2​U′+n​Un−1​U′′+ε​g​(U,U′,−c​U′,ε))′=0.\displaystyle=(-cU+aU^{n}+n(n-1)U^{n-2}U^{\prime}+nU^{n-1}U^{\prime\prime}+\varepsilon g(U,U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)\big)^{\prime}=0.

Thus, we need to find solutions of the second order ODE

−c​U+a​Un+n⁡(n−1)​Un−2​U′+n​Un−1​U′′+ε​g​(U,U′,−c​U′,ε)=k-cU+aU^{n}+n(n-1)U^{n-2}U^{\prime}+nU^{n-1}U^{\prime\prime}+\varepsilon g(U,U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)=k

with k∈ℝ.k\in\mathbb{R}. It writes as the planar system

{x′=y,y′=k+c​x−a​xn−n⁡(n−1)​xn−2​y2n​xn−1+ε​gc​(x,y,ε)n​xn−1,\left\{\!\begin{array}[]{l}x^{\prime}=y,\\[10.0pt] y^{\prime}=\dfrac{k+cx-ax^{n}-n(n-1)x^{n-2}y^{2}}{nx^{n-1}}+\varepsilon\dfrac{g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon)}{nx^{n-1}},\end{array}\right.

where gc​(x,y,ε)=−g⁡(x,y,−c​y,ε).g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon)=-g(x,y,-cy,\varepsilon). With the new time τ,\tau, where d​τ/d​s=sc,k​(x,y)d\tau/ds=s_{c,k}(x,y) and sc,k​(x,y)=x2​(1−n)/n,s_{c,k}(x,y)=x^{2(1-n)}/n, we get x=U⁡(τ)x=U(\tau) satisfies the equivalent planar ODE

{x˙=∂Hc,k​(x,y)∂y,y˙=−∂Hc,k​(x,y)∂x+ε​xn−1​gc​(x,y,ε),\begin{cases}\dot{x}=\phantom{-}\dfrac{\partial H_{c,k}(x,y)}{\partial y},\\[10.0pt] \dot{y}=-\dfrac{\partial H_{c,k}(x,y)}{\partial x}+\varepsilon x^{n-1}g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon),\end{cases}

where

Hc,k​(x,y)=n2​x2​(n−1)​y2−kn​xn−cn+1​xn+1+a2​n​x2​n.H_{c,k}(x,y)=\frac{n}{2}x^{2(n-1)}y^{2}-\frac{k}{n}x^{n}-\frac{c}{n+1}x^{n+1}+\frac{a}{2n}x^{2n}.

By Lemma 4.1 (see the comment below its statement), if there exists a singular point (x∗,0)(x_{*},0) such that

∂2Hc,k∂x2​(x∗,0)=x∗n−2​(a⁡(2​n−1)​x∗n−c​n​x∗−k⁡(n−1))>0,\frac{\partial^{2}H_{c,k}}{\partial x^{2}}(x_{*},0)=x_{*}^{n-2}\left(a\,(2n-1)\,x_{*}^{n}-c\,n\,x_{*}-k\,(n-1)\right)>0,

then it is a center. Furthermore, since the Hypothesis of Proposition 3.1 are satisfied, we can apply Theorem B and the periodic TWS for the perturbed PDE correspond to simple zeroes of

Mc,k​(h)=∫γc,k​(h)xn−1​gc​(x,y,0)​𝑑xM_{c,k}(h)=\int_{\gamma_{c,k}(h)}x^{n-1}g_{c}(x,y,0)\,dx

in a suitable interval of the energy. To get examples of perturbations with several simple zeroes we can apply Theorem C.

4.2.3. Camassa-Holm equation and related PDE

The Camassa-Holm equation is a model for the propagation of shallow water waves of moderate amplitude. The horizontal component of the fluid velocity field at a certain depth within the fluid is described by the PDE

ut+(2​κ+3​u)​ux−2​ux​ux​x+u​ux​x​x−ux​x​t=0,u_{t}+(2\kappa+3u)u_{x}-2u_{x}u_{xx}+uu_{xxx}-u_{xxt}=0,

and the parameter κ\kappa is positive. Constantin and Lannes derived in [7] a similar PDE for surface waves also with moderate amplitude in the shallow water regime,

ut+(1+6​u−6​u2+12​u3)​ux+28​ux​ux​x+14​u​ux​x​x+ux​x​x−ux​x​t=0,u_{t}+\big(1+6u-6u^{2}+12u^{3})u_{x}+28u_{x}u_{xx}+14uu_{xxx}+u_{xxx}-u_{xxt}=0,

see also [10]. Similarly, the Degasperis-Procesi equation

ut+4​u​ux−3​ux​ux​x−u​ux​x​x−ux​x​t=0,u_{t}+4uu_{x}-3u_{x}u_{xx}-uu_{xxx}-u_{xxt}=0,

which was derived initially only for its integrability properties, has a similar role in hydrodynamics.

In fact, perturbations of the above equations can be written under the common expression

ut+A′​(u)​ux+b​ux​ux​x+d​u​ux​x​x+pux​x​x+qux​x​t+rux​t​t+sut​t​t+ε∇g(u,ux,ut,ε)⋅(ux,ux​x,ux​t,0)t=0,u_{t}+A^{\prime}(u)u_{x}+bu_{x}u_{xx}+duu_{xxx}\\ +pu_{xxx}+qu_{xxt}+ru_{xtt}+su_{ttt}+\varepsilon\nabla g(u,u_{x},u_{t},\varepsilon)\cdot(u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xt},0)^{t}=0,

where AA is sufficiently smooth and b,d,p,q,rb,d,p,q,r and ss are real parameters. Its associated third order ODE is

−c​U′+A′​(U)​U′+b​U′​U′′\displaystyle-cU^{\prime}+A^{\prime}(U)U^{\prime}+bU^{\prime}U^{\prime\prime}
+dUU′′′+CU′′′+ε∇g(U,U′,−cU′,ε)⋅(U′,U′′,−cU′′,0)t\displaystyle\hskip 113.81102pt+dUU^{\prime\prime\prime}+CU^{\prime\prime\prime}+\varepsilon\nabla g(U,U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)\cdot(U^{\prime},U^{\prime\prime},-cU^{\prime\prime},0)^{t}
=(Ac​(U)+b​(U′)2/2+d⁡(U​U′′−(U′)2/2)+C​U′′+ε​g​(U,U′,−c​U′,ε))′=0\displaystyle=\Big(A_{c}(U)+b(U^{\prime})^{2}/2+d\big(UU^{\prime\prime}-(U^{\prime})^{2}/2\big)+CU^{\prime\prime}+\varepsilon g(U,U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)\Big)^{\prime}=0

where Ac​(U)=A⁡(U)−c​U,A_{c}(U)=A(U)-cU, with Ac​(0)=0,A_{c}(0)=0, and C=p−q​c+r​c2−s​c3.C=p-qc+rc^{2}-sc^{3}. Hence, for any function UU satisfying the previous equation, there exists k∈ℝ,k\in\mathbb{R}, such that

Ac​(U)+β​(U′)2+(C+d​U)​U′′+ε​g​(U,U′,−c​U′,ε)=k,A_{c}(U)+\beta(U^{\prime})^{2}+(C+dU)U^{\prime\prime}+\varepsilon g(U,U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon)=k,

where β=(b−d)/2.\beta=(b-d)/2. The above equation can be written as the planar system

{x′=y,y′=k−Ac​(x)−β​y2+ε​gc​(x,y,ε)C+d​x,\begin{cases}x^{\prime}=y,\\[10.0pt] y^{\prime}=\dfrac{k-A_{c}(x)-\beta y^{2}+\varepsilon g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon)}{C+dx},\end{cases}

where gc​(x,y,ε)=−g⁡(U,U′,−c​U′,ε).g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon)=-g(U,U^{\prime},-cU^{\prime},\varepsilon). Then, taking d​τ/d​s=sc​(x),d\tau/ds=s_{c}(x),

sc​(x)={(C+dx)−2β/dwhend≠0,e−2βx/Cwhend=0,s_{c}(x)=\begin{cases}(C+dx)^{-2\beta/d}\quad&\mbox{when}\quad d\neq 0,\\ e^{-2\beta x/C}\quad&\mbox{when}\quad d=0,\end{cases}

we get

{x˙=∂Hc,k​(x,y)∂y,y˙=−∂Hc,k​(x,y)∂x+ε​gc​(x,y,ε)(C+d​x)​sc​(x),\begin{cases}\dot{x}=\phantom{-}\dfrac{\partial H_{c,k}(x,y)}{\partial y},\\[10.0pt] \dot{y}=-\dfrac{\partial H_{c,k}(x,y)}{\partial x}+\varepsilon\dfrac{g_{c}(x,y,\varepsilon)}{(C+dx)s_{c}(x)},\end{cases}

with

Hc,k​(x,y)=y22​sc​(x)+∫0xAc​(w)−k(C+d​w)​sc​(w)​𝑑w.H_{c,k}(x,y)=\frac{y^{2}}{2s_{c}(x)}+\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{A_{c}(w)-k}{(C+dw)s_{c}(w)}\,dw.

By Lemma 4.1, any singular point (x∗,0)(x_{*},0) such that Hx​x​(x∗,0)>0,H_{xx}(x_{*},0)>0, is a center. So by Theorem B, the periodic TWS of the perturbed equations correspond with the simple zeros of

Mc.k​(h)=∫γc,k​(h)gc​(x,y,0)(C+d​x)​sc​(x)​𝑑x.M_{c.k}(h)=\int_{\gamma_{c,k}(h)}\dfrac{g_{c}(x,y,0)}{(C+dx)s_{c}(x)}\,dx.

Again, for some particular examples, the zeroes of the above type of Abelian integrals can be obtained by using Theorem C. For instance, we observe that this is trivially the case if gc​(x,y,0)=(C+d​x)​sc​(x)​(∑i=0ℓd2​i+1​y2​i+1)g_{c}(x,y,0)=(C+dx)s_{c}(x)\left(\sum_{i=0}^{\ell}d_{2i+1}y^{2i+1}\right).

4.2.4. Boussinesq-type equations

The Boussinesq equation describes bi-directional surface water waves and reads

ut​t+u​ux​x−ux​x+(ux)2−ux​x​x​x=0.u_{tt}+uu_{xx}-u_{xx}+(u_{x})^{2}-u_{xxxx}=0.

Similarly, the modified Boussinesq equation is

ut​t+u​ux​x−ux​x+(ux)2−ux​x​t​t=0,u_{tt}+uu_{xx}-u_{xx}+(u_{x})^{2}-u_{xxtt}=0,

and appears in the modelling of non-linear waves in a weakly dispersive medium. We consider the following perturbation of the family of PDE

(16) a​ux​x+b​ux​t+d​ut​t+2​e​(u​ux​x+(ux)2)+p​ux​x​x​x+q​ux​x​x​t+r​ux​x​t​t+s​ux​t​t​t+f​ut​t​t​t+ε​G=0,au_{xx}+bu_{xt}+du_{tt}+2e(uu_{xx}+(u_{x})^{2})\\ +pu_{xxxx}+qu_{xxxt}+ru_{xxtt}+su_{xttt}+fu_{tttt}+\varepsilon G=0,

, where a,b,d,e,p,q,r,s,fa,b,d,e,p,q,r,s,f are suitable real parameters. We do not detail here the perturbation G,G, but it is a function of all the partial derivatives of uu up to order four, and such that after replacing uu by U⁡(x−c​t)U(x-ct) it holds that there exists a function gcg_{c} such that G=(gc​(U,U′,ε))′′.G=\big(g_{c}(U,U^{\prime},\varepsilon)\big)^{\prime\prime}. Hence the ODE associated to (16) is

C​U′′+e​(U2)′′+D​U′′′′+ε​(gc​(U,U′,ε))′′=(C​U+e​U2+D​U′′+ε​gc​(U,U′,ε))′′=0,CU^{\prime\prime}+e(U^{2})^{\prime\prime}+DU^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}+\varepsilon\big(g_{c}(U,U^{\prime},\varepsilon)\big)^{\prime\prime}=\big(CU+eU^{2}+DU^{\prime\prime}+\varepsilon g_{c}(U,U^{\prime},\varepsilon)\big)^{\prime\prime}=0,

where C=a−b​c+d2​c,C=a-bc+d^{2}c, D=p−q​c+r​c2−s​c3+f​c4,D=p-qc+rc^{2}-sc^{3}+fc^{4}, and we have used that (u2)x​x=2​u​ux+2​(ux)2.(u^{2})_{xx}=2uu_{x}+2(u_{x})^{2}. We are interested in solutions of the above fourth order ODE

(17) C​U+e​U2+D​U′′+ε​gc​(U,U′,ε)=k,CU+eU^{2}+DU^{\prime\prime}+\varepsilon g_{c}(U,U^{\prime},\varepsilon)=k,

for some k∈ℝ.k\in\mathbb{R}. When D≠0D\neq 0 we are again under the situation covered by Theorem B. Notice that other solutions would satisfy C​U+e​U2+D​U′′+ε​gc​(U,U′,ε)=k1​s+k2,CU+eU^{2}+DU^{\prime\prime}+\varepsilon g_{c}(U,U^{\prime},\varepsilon)=k_{1}s+k_{2}, for some k1≠0,k2∈ℝ,k_{1}\neq 0,k_{2}\in\mathbb{R}, but we do not consider them. In fact, from (17) we arrive at the same ODE that appears in the study done in Section 4.2.1 about the perturbed generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation, but with a different notation. Indeed, the above ODE is the same as (15) and it can be studied to get TWS for (16) exactly like in that case.
